regions.name: Middle East
overview: The US-Iran maritime confrontation returned to open kinetic exchange after a roughly five-week lull: US strike waves on southern Iran and Strait of Hormuz coastal infrastructure (Larak Island 30 August; a multi-site salvo across Hormozgan on 1 September) drew the largest Iranian retaliation in months, with IRGC 'Punishment of the Aggressor' ballistic-missile and drone strikes on US bases in Jordan, Bahrain, Iraq and Kuwait.

The Strait of Hormuz is now the epicentre: tankers were struck off Oman and near Yanbu, visible transits collapsed to a handful of vessels a day, and Brent rose more than 4% on the week — while previously insulated Gulf states were hit for the first time, turning the peninsula's US basing network into one contiguous battlespace and justifying Jordan's upgrade to CRITICAL.

Every 'frozen' sub-state track is degrading in parallel: Gaza's post-truce toll passed roughly 1,288 and triggered an Israeli general strike over hostages; Lebanon's LAF disarmament milestone lapsed on 31 August with Hezbollah drones back over the ridge line; Yemen's civil-war fronts reignited around Marib; and Iraq faces a 30 September militia-disarmament deadline its government cannot enforce.

Sunni jihadist and communal violence persists as a secondary vector — renewed Suwayda clashes in Syria and ISIS-style attacks on Syrian security forces — while peripheral governance crises deepen: Tunisia protests into a third month amid a second near-50°C heatwave and utility collapse, and Libya's GNU-GNS deadlock hardens toward permanence.

countries.name: Gaza
incidents: 31 Aug — Gaza City: Israeli strikes across Gaza killed at least five, including two near a municipal park in Gaza City.

1 Sep — Rimal, Gaza City: An Israeli special-forces raid captured Hamas security official Muein al-Arabid amid accompanying strikes; the same day a girl was shot dead by Israeli ground forces near the Yellow Line in Deir al-Balah.
2 Sep — Gaza City: An Israeli strike killed Hamas Gaza City Brigade commander Talal Badawi and a second operative; the IDF cited a 'systematic violation of the ceasefire.'
1 Sep — Gaza: The post-truce Palestinian death toll reached about 1,288 (Gaza Health Ministry) as the October 2025 ceasefire held in name only.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. The October 2025 ceasefire persists only nominally: expect the near-daily strike tempo and creeping Yellow Line consolidation to continue, punctuated by ground raids to seize or kill Hamas cadre. The recovery of executed hostages' bodies and the 2 September Histadrut general strike have sharpened domestic Israeli pressure on Netanyahu, making a partial hostages-for-pause deal the most likely near-term inflection; absent that, incremental annexation of Yellow Line areas and throttled humanitarian access continue. A mass-casualty strike on a shelter or aid site remains the principal trigger for a formal collapse or a renewed high-intensity operation.

countries.name: Lebanon
incidents: 31 Aug — Arnoun / Ali al-Taher ridge: Hezbollah launched two explosive drones at IDF troops with no casualties; Israel conducted retaliatory strikes and detonations near Arnoun.

31 Aug — Beirut: The Lebanese Armed Forces' first-phase Hezbollah-disarmament milestone lapsed with no Hezbollah compliance; the army cited legal limits on searching private homes and continued Israeli strikes.
2 Sep — Nabatieh: An Israeli drone strike killed one person and wounded another.
1 Sep — Washington / Beirut: Netanyahu met US envoy Huckabee ahead of an eighth round of US-mediated Lebanon-Israel talks, with a further Rome session reported for mid-September.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. The June framework is functionally dead: Hezbollah has resumed limited drone harassment along the ridge line and will not proceed to phase-two disarmament while Israel occupies southern positions and strikes at will. Expect the Rome track to continue as a low-yield holding mechanism while Israel sustains its strike campaign and its five hilltop positions. The realistic 90-day path is continued tit-for-tat below the threshold of the 2024 war, with escalation risk concentrated in a Hezbollah strike that kills IDF soldiers or an Israeli strike into Beirut's southern suburbs.

countries.name: Iran
incidents: 30 Aug — Larak Island: A US strike hit IRGC rocket launchers and sea drones, with Iranian state media reporting two killed; the stated aim was to prevent Hormuz mine-laying.
1 Sep — Hormozgan (Kuhestak, Sirik, Bandar Abbas, Jask, Qeshm): A simultaneous US strike wave killed about 11, including civilians, and wounded dozens.
30 Aug – 1 Sep — Regional: The IRGC's 'Punishment of the Aggressor' campaign struck US bases in Jordan, Bahrain, Iraq and Kuwait with missiles and drones.

2 Sep — Tehran: The rial fell to about 2.2 million per US dollar; the Supreme National Security Council threatened a new 'battlefield, diplomacy and economic' strategy as the UN snapback-sanctions dispute stayed unresolved.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. The confrontation has settled into a strike-counterstrike equilibrium centred on Hormuz: the US hits coastal missile, radar and mine-laying infrastructure, Iran answers with salvos at Gulf bases and tankers, and neither has yet struck a regime-threatening target. Economic collapse — the rial in freefall, snapback sanctions contested at the Security Council — is the more dangerous vector, raising the odds of domestic unrest and repression on the December 2025 scale. Expect continued cyclical exchanges, a possible Omani or Pakistani-brokered maritime de-confliction attempt, and a persistent low probability of a US strike on a higher-value target that breaks the equilibrium.

countries.name: Yemen
incidents: 28 Aug — Marib / Hadramawt / Taiz: Houthi-government fighting intensified across multiple fronts as government forces pressed a 'decisive offensive,' including Republican Guard advances near Mokha.
24 Aug – 1 Sep — Red Sea: The Houthis stayed silent for roughly eight days after the 24 August ballistic-missile strike on the Saudi VLCC Amzan, issuing no claims during the US-Iran exchange.
31 Aug — Red Sea: The Bahri-operated tanker Sidr was reportedly attacked outside the usual Houthi operating area; no claim was made.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Two overlapping wars continue — the reignited Houthi-government civil war around Marib, Hadramawt and Taiz, and the Houthi campaign against Saudi Arabia and Red Sea shipping. The one-week Red Sea and Saudi lull is most likely tactical resupply and repositioning rather than de-escalation; expect renewed strikes on Saudi energy nodes (Jazan, Yanbu) and Bahri tankers within the horizon. A Saudi ground offensive remains possible but risky; the likelier path is continued Saudi air and interception operations plus the 13-nation Jeddah maritime coalition, with the civil-war fronts grinding without decisive movement.

countries.name: Israel
incidents: 29 Aug — Qusra / Jalud, West Bank: Settlers occupied a Palestinian home in Qusra; a separate settler attack targeted an NBC News crew near Jalud.
1 Sep — Bazzariya, West Bank: A settler arson attack hit a village mosque; the IDF dismissed a reservist commander who had prayed with settlers at the Qusra outpost but made no arrests.
2 Sep — al-Mughayyir / Qusra / Beita, West Bank: Settler-and-IDF incursions killed two Palestinians, both 19, and wounded three.
2 Sep — Israel: The Histadrut labour federation joined mass hostage-deal protests with a general strike; hundreds of thousands demonstrated.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Settler violence in the northern West Bank — the Qusra, Jalud and Mughayyir corridor — is escalating with de facto state tolerance and driving further village displacement; expect the pattern of raids, arson and shooting deaths to continue alongside E1 construction advancing. The hostage issue is now the dominant domestic fault line and could force a government crisis or an early-election dynamic within the window. The compounding risk is a West Bank mass-casualty event — a settler pogrom or a major Palestinian attack — that triggers a broader IDF operation or a third-intifada dynamic.

countries.name: Iraq
incidents: 1 Sep — Erbil province: An IRGC missile-and-drone strike hit US-linked facilities, with Iran claiming a destroyed repair centre and warehouses and fuel tanks set alight.
Through the window — Baghdad: The government's 30 September deadline for pro-Iran militias to disarm neared, with Badr's Hadi al-Ameri warning that a coercive campaign could 'ignite civil war.'
17 Aug — Pirmam, Erbil: The earlier Iranian drone strike on the KRG prime minister's office remained formally unclaimed.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Iraq is being pulled onto the war's frontline from two directions: as a platform for Iranian retaliation against US facilities in Erbil, and internally via the 30 September disarmament deadline. Baghdad almost certainly cannot disarm Kataib Hezbollah or Nujaba by force without provoking intra-Shia conflict, so expect a face-saving partial agreement, continued militia autonomy, and sporadic strikes on Erbil and on US logistics. The KRG leadership remains a target set; a militia strike that kills US personnel is the main trigger for direct US action on Iraqi soil.

countries.name: Saudi Arabia
incidents: 24 Aug – 1 Sep — Southern border / Red Sea: No new Houthi strike hit Saudi territory or shipping, an eight-day lull since the ballistic-missile strike on the Amzan off Yanbu.
2 Sep — Markets: Brent rose more than 4% after the US strike wave on Iran; Saudi energy infrastructure remains the Houthis' principal escalation lever.
Ongoing — Red Sea: The 13-nation Jeddah maritime coalition is operating as Riyadh continues to weigh a Yemen ground offensive.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained (a quiet week, but strategic exposure unchanged). The calm is likely a Houthi operational pause rather than a shift; expect resumed strikes on Jazan and Yanbu energy nodes and Red Sea tankers, with Patriot, THAAD and coalition interception keeping most attacks non-catastrophic. Riyadh's dilemma persists: a ground offensive into Yemen risks a drawn-out war and heavier retaliation, so the base case is continued air defence, coalition escorts and quiet de-escalation signalling via Oman. A successful Houthi strike on Abqaiq-class infrastructure or a crewed tanker casualty is the scenario that forces a Saudi offensive.

countries.name: Syria
incidents: 30 Aug – 1 Sep — Suwayda: Renewed clashes between Damascus-aligned forces and Sheikh al-Hijri's Druze factions killed at least two civilians.
25 Aug — Northeast Syria: SDF commander Mazloum Abdi declared the force's integration into the Syrian army complete and announced the SDF's dissolution.
Through Aug — Southern Syria: Sporadic Israeli strikes and overflights continued near Beit Jinn amid the unresolved Israel-Turkey standoff over Turkish deployment to Syrian bases.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Two dynamics dominate: Suwayda remains the last major zone outside Damascus's control and is the likeliest flashpoint for a government offensive that draws renewed Israeli intervention on 'protect the Druze' grounds; and the Israel-Turkey contest over Turkish basing keeps a great-power collision risk live. SDF integration removes one fault line but its implementation in the northeast could still fracture. Expect continued Israeli strikes on any perceived Turkish or strategic-weapons movement, episodic Suwayda violence, periodic jihadist bombings in Damascus and Homs, and a low but real chance of an Israel-Turkey direct incident.

countries.name: Egypt
incidents: No kinetic incident occurred on Egyptian soil in the window.
2 Sep — Cairo: Xi Jinping met President Sisi, signing a Suez Canal industrial-zone phase-3 agreement and calling for a 'new Middle East security framework.'
Through Aug — Suez Canal: Transits remained roughly 50–60% below normal as EASA conflict-zone bulletins widened to cover much of the western Gulf.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Egypt stays off the kinetic map but absorbs mounting economic damage from Suez revenue loss and regional shipping avoidance, now partly offset by deepening Chinese investment in the canal zone. The main security risks are indirect: spillover from a Gaza escalation into Rafah and Sinai, a stray missile or drone during a Hormuz-Red Sea exchange, or renewed Houthi targeting of Bab al-Mandeb traffic that further chokes the canal. The base case is continued heightened alert around the canal and the Sumed pipeline without a direct strike; a second attack on Egyptian soil would warrant immediate re-elevation.

countries.name: Jordan
incidents: 30 Aug — King Hussein Air Base / Al Azraq: An IRGC missile and drone salvo targeted US-used bases; Jordan intercepted eight missiles that breached its airspace, with no injuries.

1 Sep — Prince Hassan Air Base / near Aqaba: Iranian ballistic missiles targeted a US Marine site and hangars housing US drones; Jordan intercepted 10 of 13, with the rest falling on open ground and no casualties.
Through the window — Jordanian airspace: Repeated violations heavily disrupted commercial aviation, with EASA advising carriers to avoid Jordanian airspace.
countries.coa: Upgraded to CRITICAL from HIGH. Jordanian territory was directly struck by Iranian ballistic missiles twice in the window and US bases on Jordanian soil are now active retaliation targets, ending the July-August kinetic lull that justified the earlier downgrade. Jordan can expect further salvos each time Washington strikes Iran, with Jordanian and US air defence intercepting most but not all incoming. Amman will keep publicly protesting both US strikes launched near its territory and Iranian violations while quietly hosting US defensive assets. Principal risks: a missile leaking through onto a populated area, debris casualties, or domestic unrest over the Kingdom's perceived alignment.

countries.name: Libya
incidents: No verified kinetic incident occurred in the window.

Late Aug — Tripoli: The GNU-GNS deadlock over election legislation persisted; UNSMIL delivered its 60-day Security Council briefing, with militia rivalry over security appointments the main flashpoint.
12 Jul — Gatrun, southern Libya: A rebel attack on an LNA checkpoint remains the most recent confirmed southern flashpoint.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. Libya stays in its calm-tension holding pattern: political division hardening toward permanence, no active front, but Tripoli militia coalitions one contested appointment away from renewed street fighting of the kind seen in 2023 and May 2026. Expect continued mobilisation cycles, possible short clashes in the capital, and stable-but-fragile oil production. A return to sustained west-east conflict is unlikely within the horizon absent a major external trigger; watch for a triggering assassination or checkpoint incident and periodic southern clashes linked to cross-border militia activity from Niger and Chad.

countries.name: Tunisia
incidents: Late Aug — Kairouan / nationwide: A second major heatwave near 50°C (Kairouan 49.8°C) caused deaths and prolonged power and water cuts, feeding public anger.
20 Aug — Tunis: Hundreds protested for a second consecutive month demanding President Saied's ouster and a return to democratic rule.
Ongoing — Nationwide: The crackdown on opposition figures, journalists and civil society continued, with Ennahda leaders still detained.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. Tunisia's trajectory is slow authoritarian consolidation amid economic decay rather than acute crisis. Expect the monthly non-violent protest cycle to continue and possibly grow as utility failures and inflation bite, met by more detentions rather than concessions. The risk is a tipping-point event — a death in custody, a security-force crackdown on a large protest, or a bread or subsidy shock — that converts diffuse discontent into sustained unrest; short of that, the status quo holds.

regions.name: Ukraine/Russia
overview: The air war stepped up sharply: the 28 August Russian strike on an ammunition depot at Myla near Kyiv killed 38 — the deadliest attack of 2026 — and Kyiv absorbed six straight nights of drone and missile barrages (roughly 2,000 drones, 1,600 glide bombs and 31 missiles in one week), with Ukrainian intelligence warning of an imminent Russian campaign against the power grid before the fourth war winter.

Ukraine's deep-strike campaign is measurably degrading Russia: a record 21 refinery strikes in August drove Russian refining to a 20-year low, the No. 2 Kirishi plant was hit 29–30 August, fuel rationing now spans 50-plus regions and the diesel and marine-fuel export ban was extended to 30 September; roughly 8,670 drones were launched at the Moscow region in August alone.

The ground front is effectively frozen: ISW assesses Russia's spring-summer offensive failed to achieve operational manoeuvre, gaining only marginal ground at a high and rising casualty rate for a second consecutive month.

No diplomatic movement: Putin and Zelensky traded escalation threats over 1–2 September, Moscow again rejected a ceasefire and a leaders' summit, and Putin used the SCO summit in Tianjin and the 3 September Beijing WWII parade alongside Xi and Kim to project confidence that he can outlast Western support for Kyiv.

countries.name: Ukraine
incidents: 28–29 Aug — Myla, Kyiv Oblast: A Russian drone strike on an ammunition warehouse set off hours of secondary explosions in a residential area; the toll rose to 38, the war's deadliest single attack of 2026.
31 Aug — Kyiv: A sixth consecutive night of jet-powered Shahed and missile attacks killed at least 12 in the capital and suburbs, including six railway workers at a rail depot.
1 Sep — Kyiv / Boryspil: Strikes on the first day of the school year killed at least four and wounded more than 13, including three children.

2 Sep — Kyiv / Dnipro / Odesa: Combined strikes killed two in Dnipro and wounded up to 13 in Kyiv; power outages hit five regions as Zelensky warned of 'very troubling' intelligence on a coming Russian campaign against the grid.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained, compounding. Expect Russia to open a concentrated strike campaign on generation and grid nodes through September-November, timed to the heating season and exploiting continued Ukrainian interceptor scarcity; mass Shahed and decoy salvos combined with ballistic 'leaker' tactics will keep urban casualty tolls high. Ground lines stay largely static, with grinding Russian pressure around Pokrovsk, Kostiantynivka and Kupyansk at rising cost. The decisive internal variable is the NABU/SAP corruption probe now reaching into the Presidential Office, which with Fedorov-aligned protest activity remains the main risk to political cohesion. No ceasefire is likely this quarter; Kyiv will keep pressing for a leaders' summit and deepening its deep-strike campaign as its principal coercive lever.

countries.name: Russia
incidents: Through the window — 50-plus regions: The fuel crisis deepened after a record 21 refinery drone strikes in August; refining fell to a 20-year low and the diesel and marine-fuel export ban was extended to 30 September.

29–30 Aug — Kirishi, Leningrad Oblast: A Ukrainian long-range strike set ablaze the KINEF refinery, Russia's second-largest, alongside hits on a drone site in Rostov Oblast and an airfield in Krasnodar Krai.

31 Aug – 1 Sep — Moscow region: One of the largest drone attacks yet on the capital; Russia reported 239 drones downed over 14 regions overnight, and the mayor said about 8,670 drones flew toward the Moscow region during August.
31 Aug – 3 Sep — Tianjin / Beijing: Putin met Xi, attended the SCO summit and joined Xi and Kim Jong Un at the 3 September Beijing military parade in a staged demonstration of anti-Western alignment.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. The Kremlin will keep absorbing the economic cost — extending export bans, shuffling fuel between regions and importing from Belarus — while avoiding formal rationing acknowledgements; localised shortages, price spikes and sporadic regional discontent are likely to persist into winter without becoming regime-threatening. Militarily, Moscow doubles down on the strike campaign against Ukraine's grid and on incremental Donetsk gains rather than a new axis. Diplomatically, Putin banks the SCO and Beijing optics and Chinese and North Korean backing to signal he can outlast Western support for Kyiv; expect continued rejection of a Putin-Zelensky meeting and of US 'Article 5-like' guarantee proposals in their current form. Black Sea export and insurer disruption will keep pressuring Russian and Kazakh crude flows.

countries.name: Belarus
incidents: Through Aug — Gomel region: Incremental militarisation near the Ukrainian border continued, including formation of the 37th Separate Air Assault Brigade about 40 km from the frontier.
Through the window — EU border: Belarus sustained hybrid migration pressure on Lithuania and Poland alongside the US-Minsk prisoner-release and sanctions-relief track.
September — Regional: A Zapad-2026 strategic exercise cycle is anticipated in the month, with no confirmed dates or scale as of early September.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. Belarus remains a facilitation and pressure platform rather than a direct belligerent. Expect Minsk to host and enable any autumn Russian exercise activity, sustain calibrated migration pressure on the EU border, and continue trading political-prisoner releases for incremental Western sanctions relief. A Zapad-2026 iteration, if held, will drive temporary NATO border closures and heightened eastern-flank alert but is unlikely to presage offensive action. The 37th Air Assault Brigade warrants monitoring for any shift from garrison to forward posture; direct Belarusian combat entry stays low-probability.

countries.name: Moldova
incidents: Through the window — Nationwide: President Sandu and officials warned of an 'unprecedented' Kremlin interference campaign — illicit financing including crypto, vote-buying, cyberattacks and coordinated TikTok, Telegram and Facebook disinformation — ahead of the 28 September parliamentary election.
Through Aug — Transnistria: The Russian troop presence of about 1,500 and the frozen energy and passportisation dynamic were unchanged, with no new escalation.
Late Aug — International press: Continued reporting detailed Russia's large-scale hybrid operation against Moldova.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained, with the next four weeks the peak-risk period. Expect a disinformation and vote-buying surge, probable cyber incidents against electoral infrastructure, bomb-threat harassment of diaspora polling, and Moscow-cued street-mobilisation attempts around and after the 28 September vote. PAS is polling first but may fall short of a governing majority, raising the prospect of a contested result and a coalition scramble Russia will seek to exploit — a scenario that would justify re-elevation to HIGH. Transnistria stays a latent lever rather than an active front; kinetic escalation risk remains low but non-trivial.

countries.name: Georgia
incidents: 31 Aug — Tbilisi: The 37th consecutive Saturday pro-EU march took place; Amnesty International welcomed the pardon of nine jailed protesters but said 'pardons cannot replace justice.'
1 Sep — Tbilisi: Parliament's autumn session opened with Georgian Dream alone; three people were detained over the death of Abkhaz blogger Daur Buava.

2 Sep — Tbilisi: Former PM Irakli Garibashvili publicly accused the Georgian Dream leadership of involvement in deaths officially ruled suicides; a businessman was arrested during an apartment search.
Ongoing — Tbilisi: Daily protests passed roughly 640 days as the opposition split over whether to boycott the 4 October local elections.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Georgian Dream will use the boycott-fractured October local elections to claim a clean sweep and further entrench control of municipal institutions, then likely move to restrict or ban boycotting opposition parties citing 'election-day unrest.' Expect a spike in protest turnout and police confrontation around 4 October, followed by a renewed crackdown — arrests, fines, possible new legislation — with 50-plus political prisoners already held. EU accession stays frozen and a visa-suspension review is due by March 2027. The protest movement persists but without a unifying strategy; a negotiated off-ramp is improbable this quarter.

countries.name: Armenia
incidents: 1 Sep — Bishkek: Pashinyan met Aliyev on the SCO sidelines for further normalisation talks on trade, energy and connectivity; Armenia announced the start of direct bilateral trade with Azerbaijan.
2 Sep — Bishkek: Pashinyan met Putin, who publicly urged Armenia to hold a referendum on EU versus EAEU membership; Pashinyan said 'the question is not yet ripe.'
3 Sep — Brussels: The EU approved enhanced GSP+ trade preferences for Armenia, a step that could redirect the bulk of Armenian agricultural and beverage exports away from Russia.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Armenia continues a deliberate westward reorientation — EU trade integration, distance from the CSTO, and step-by-step normalisation with Baku and Ankara — while managing Russian economic retaliation risk via gas, nuclear fuel, remittances, roughly $12bn in bilateral trade and the 102nd base. Moscow will escalate pressure short of direct coercion: propaganda, the referendum demand, leverage over the Russian border guard, expanded trade bans and support for domestic opposition and Church-aligned actors ahead of Armenia's 2026 parliamentary contest. The Azerbaijan track is the stabiliser; a formal peace-treaty signing is possible this quarter though implementation remains contested.

countries.name: Azerbaijan
incidents: 1 Sep — Bishkek: Aliyev and Putin held their first substantive conversation since relations went into 'freefall,' a tentative de-escalation gesture over the December 2024 airliner crash, Russian strikes on SOCAR assets in Ukraine and closed Russian cultural centres.
31 Aug — Baku: Azerbaijan's foreign ministry protested a Polish TVP broadcast over its coverage of the country.
In the window — Baku: Azerbaijani outlets floated that Baku 'may consider lifting its arms embargo on Ukraine,' signalling continued alignment against Moscow.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. The Aliyev-Putin meeting is a managed pause, not a reconciliation. Baku keeps ties with Moscow cold but stable-managed: no formal rupture, but continued needling — support signals to Ukraine, protection of the Azerbaijani diaspora in Russia as a grievance, and assertive messaging on Karabakh and sovereignty. The Armenia peace process is the main positive vector; expect Aliyev to press for constitutional concessions from Yerevan and movement on the Zangezur corridor as the price of a treaty. Principal risk: a fresh incident involving Azerbaijani nationals in Russia, or another Russian strike on SOCAR infrastructure in Ukraine, tipping the relationship from cold to openly hostile.

regions.name: Sahel
overview: Junta survival is now externally underwritten: Niger's 28–29 August coup attempt — the first serious armed challenge to an AES government — was put down only by Russian Africa Corps ground troops and Algerian air support, even though the mutineers came from units bled fighting jihadists; all three juntas will emerge more coup-wary, more repressive internally and more dependent on Moscow.

Jihadist economic warfare has become the decisive instrument: JNIM's Mali fuel blockade passed its one-year mark on 3 September with Kayes and Nioro du Sahel sealed and Bamako rationing fuel, while the JNIM-ISSP fratricidal war keeps redrawing control across the Mali-Burkina-Niger tri-border, much of it masked by Burkina Faso's near-total reporting blackout.

The Sudan war is now a Sahel-wide driver: two acknowledged Sudanese strikes inside Chad in one week (Ennedi Est; the Adikoun fuel market, 12 killed) have N'Djamena on maximum military alert, West Darfur fighting is pushing roughly 18,000 refugees a week into eastern Chad, and El Obeid faces an El-Fasher-style mass-atrocity risk with 200,000-plus displaced across Kordofan.

State authority keeps receding at the periphery on every axis: Nigeria's northwest (17 Katsina villages raided in days), Plateau's targeted clergy killings, a Lake Chad ISWAP revival and Chadian intercommunal violence (23 dead at Oum-Hadjer) all point to a widening governance vacuum that collapsing humanitarian funding — the Sudan appeal is about 40% financed — cannot offset.

countries.name: Mali
incidents: 28 Aug — Niger–Mali border: The Azawad Liberation Front handed 61 Malian soldiers to Nigerien authorities, its third prisoner release in August after roughly 82 on 13–14 August and 22 around 23 August.
29 Aug — Gao (Bagoundié): An explosion killed five and severely injured two; local sources attributed it to an old artillery shell being handled.
30–31 Aug — Kignan / Sikasso and Ségou regions: An attack on the Kignan police station was followed by a wave of FAMa airstrikes under 'Operation Dougoukoloko'; no casualty figures were released.

3 Sep — Kayes / Nioro du Sahel axis: The JNIM fuel blockade passed its one-year mark with both cities sealed and Bamako resupplied only by military-escorted convoys; more than 300 tankers have been destroyed since it began.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Expect the blockade to persist and tighten seasonally as the dry season opens road movement to JNIM; Bamako fuel rationing, rolling blackouts and price spikes will continue, with periodic multi-day convoy interdictions on the Senegal and Côte d'Ivoire corridors. FAMa and Africa Corps will keep substituting airstrikes and stand-off raids for ground presence, generating unverifiable body counts and episodic civilian-harm incidents that harden JNIM's narrative. The FLA prisoner releases signal a slow-moving north-south negotiation track that could produce a localised Kidal-area accommodation but will not relieve the south. Watch for JNIM converting the blockade's anniversary into a propaganda escalation and for pressure on Kayes town itself.

countries.name: Niger
incidents: 28–29 Aug — Niamey: A mutinous faction attacked Base 101, the presidential palace and state broadcaster ORTN, briefly seizing the airport and media and declaring Gen. Tiani 'no longer head of state,' dissolving the constitution and imposing a curfew.

30–31 Aug — Niamey: The Presidential Guard, reinforced by Russian Africa Corps personnel and Algerian Su-30 air support, retook Base 101; dozens of mutineers were killed or arrested and at least three guardsmen were killed.

31 Aug – 2 Sep — Niamey: Journalist Moussa Kaka was reported missing and former defence minister Kalla Moutari was detained without stated charge as authorities alleged Chadian and Bazoum-linked involvement.
15 Aug — Séguédine, Kawar region: The Toubou rebel group MPLJ attacked security positions, killing several personnel and abducting three.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained, with the basis broadening from two-front insurgency to acute regime instability — the junta survived only through foreign intervention. Expect a visible purge — arrests of officers, unit reshuffles, tighter Presidential Guard vetting, and continued detentions of Bazoum-era figures and journalists — alongside intensified information control and rising Russian Africa Corps leverage over Niamey. Border and airspace restrictions will ease within days but recur. The frontline grievance that drove the mutiny — unsustainable casualties against JNIM in Tillabéri and ISWAP and Boko Haram in Diffa — is unaddressed, so renewed unrest or a follow-on plot is a live risk. Algeria's air support marks a notable Algiers-Niamey thaw.

countries.name: Burkina Faso
incidents: In the window — Nationwide: No tier-one-verified incident surfaced; Burkina Faso maintains a near-total blackout on security reporting, so the absence of headlines reflects a reporting gap, not a lull.
Late Aug — Ouagadougou: The junta condemned the Niger coup attempt and reaffirmed AES solidarity.
17 Aug — Northeastern Burkina Faso: A JNIM ambush killed ISSP's emir for the northeast, with pro-JNIM channels warning of a large-scale retaliatory offensive.
Ongoing — North and East: JNIM sieges of Djibo, Sebba and other provincial towns continued alongside the JNIM-ISSP war concentrated on Burkinabè Liptako-Gourma.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained; the open JNIM-ISSP conflict remains the key deteriorating vector. It may temporarily divert both groups' capacity from state and civilian targets as they contest the northeast, but a decisive ISSP counter-offensive risks a fresh spike in civilian massacres as both sides punish communities suspected of aiding the rival faction. JNIM retains the initiative across the North, Sahel, Est and Boucle du Mouhoun, besieging towns and continuing punitive killings; junta VDP mobilisation will drive further abuses. The Niamey mutiny will make Ouagadougou more coup-wary and lean further on Africa Corps elements. Little prospect of territorial recovery.

countries.name: Sudan
incidents: 29 Aug — Al-Qaa and Al-Kawakiti, North Kordofan: An RSF raid west of Bara executed five young men, looted the villages and displaced more than 3,000 people, some reaching western Omdurman in critical condition.
30 Aug — Near El Obeid: SAF–RSF clashes around the North Kordofan capital killed 14, amid continued RSF drone strikes on the city's water and power infrastructure.
Past week — West Darfur: Fighting displaced about 18,000 people from more than 20 villages, most fleeing across the border into Chad.
27 Aug — Kauda, South Kordofan: SPLM-N (al-Hilu) fighting continued as Otoro constituencies publicly demanded al-Hilu's removal from the movement's leadership.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained, escalating. El Obeid is the decisive near-term flashpoint: RSF force build-up, an infrastructure-targeting drone campaign and village-clearing raids on the southwestern approaches mirror the El-Fasher siege pattern. A ground assault or a negotiated SAF withdrawal within the horizon would risk large-scale atrocities against a trapped, cholera-affected population; UN warnings of 'risk of mass atrocities' should be read as an early-warning indicator. Kordofan displacement (200,000-plus) will keep rising and push into Khartoum State and White Nile, with continued cross-border spillover into Chad. The Quad truce framework remains stalled; no ceasefire is likely in the window. SPLM-N internal fracture could open a third front in South Kordofan.

countries.name: Chad
incidents: 27 Aug — Adikoun, near the eastern frontier: An airstrike on a fuel market used by the RSF for refuelling killed 12 and wounded seven; Chad's army blamed the Sudanese armed forces and issued a 'firm warning' over escalation, which Sudan denied.
20–23 Aug — Ennedi Est (more than 100 km inside Chad): The preceding acknowledged Sudanese strike on a vehicle convoy kept Chad's military on nationwide high alert.
Late Aug — Oum-Hadjer, Batha province: An intercommunal land dispute between the Massalatte and Bichéchatte communities left 23 dead over several days before a mediated peace agreement.
19 Aug — N'Djamena: Chad publicly confirmed the rebuilding of military cooperation with France, with French troops back since April for training, intelligence and air support.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained (upgraded from HIGH the prior week). The second acknowledged strike by Sudanese state forces inside Chadian territory in a week, together with a nationwide military alert, sustains the qualitative shift from contained border spillover to direct interstate-escalation risk. Expect further cross-border incidents in Ennedi, Wadi Fira and Ouaddaï, a possible Chadian shift in air-defence posture or retaliatory strikes into Sudan, and continued refugee inflow toward the roughly one million Sudanese already sheltering in the east. French ISR and air support will expand, and the probability of a miscalculation drawing Chad directly into the war is now non-trivial; intercommunal and land-driven violence is a parallel instability stream.

countries.name: Mauritania
incidents: In the window — Nouadhibou–Canary Islands route: No new mass shipwreck or large rescue was reported, following the rescue of more than 300 people off Nouadhibou on 21 August.
2 Sep — Nationwide: The UN Special Rapporteur on the human rights of migrants began a country visit expected to report critically on arbitrary detention and expulsions under EU-backed interception.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Migrant departure volumes along the Atlantic route show no sign of abating heading into the September-November peak season, and coastguard capacity is being stretched by sustained, high-density departures from The Gambia and Senegal. Expect continued high-frequency rescue operations interspersed with periodic further fatal shipwrecks off Nouadhibou and Dakhla given persistent use of overloaded pirogues, plus continued reports of pushbacks and mass expulsions of West African migrants under EU pressure. Direct security risk to foreigners stays low; JNIM's blockade of adjacent western Mali keeps a low-level risk of border-zone incidents.

countries.name: Nigeria
incidents: 28 Aug — Bokkos LGA, Plateau State: Pastor Emmanuel Hills and a colleague were seized from a minibus south of Jos; Hills was stabbed to death and his body recovered the next day, while the colleague was freed on ransom.
From 29 Aug — Faskari LGA, Katsina State: Bandits attacked 17 villages over several days, killing residents, abducting others and looting livestock.
29 Aug — Matazu LGA, Katsina State: A JTF operation under Operation Fansan Yamma killed a bandit commander and recovered weapons.
25 Aug — Gusau–Funtua highway, Zamfara State: Gunmen ambushed motorists, killing eight, abducting eight and wounding nine; security forces later killed 17 suspected bandits in pursuit.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. The north-western kidnap-for-ransom economy across Zamfara, Katsina, Sokoto, Kebbi and Niger states will sustain mass village raids and highway ambushes despite tactical security wins, with army clearance operations producing periodic large bandit body counts without durable territorial control. Expect continued targeted killings and abductions of clergy and travellers in the Plateau and southern-Kaduna belt, and a sustained ISWAP resurgence around Lake Chad and in southern Borno. The roughly 78 Borno schoolchildren abducted in May remain a live hostage crisis and a growing political liability for Abuja; US engagement has receded to intelligence support after the mid-2026 drawdown.

regions.name: Asia-Pacific
overview: China is rebalancing coercion from air to sea: PLA incursions into Taiwan's ADIZ fell again in August (125 aircraft versus a 300-plus monthly peak in 2024) while China Coast Guard presence hit record levels at Scarborough Shoal and around Pag-asa and stayed near-daily at the Senkakus, exploiting the Western Pacific US carrier gap through persistent grey-zone pressure; the Philippines carries the highest single-incident risk.

Myanmar remains the region's deadliest conflict and is not improving: junta airstrikes killed more than 100 civilians in August and continued into September (Mindat, 30 August), resistance forces are contesting monsoon river resupply toward Bhamo, and the military-backed post-election government in Naypyitaw offers no policy change.

Pakistan's western insurgencies are at their most acute in years: the BLA sustained a high-tempo, multi-district campaign across Balochistan and 1 September operations killed more than 20 militants and six soldiers, while persistent TTP activity continues in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

Scattered de-escalation signals elsewhere, none decisive: North Korea had an operationally quiet week but expanded its force contributions to Russia and reshuffled its defence minister around the same time as South Korea; Manipur saw Kuki-Zo legislators return to the assembly but a 28 September shutdown looms; the Thailand-Cambodia ceasefire holds fragilely; and Sri Lanka is trending calm enough to consider a downgrade.

countries.name: North Korea
incidents: 30 Aug — Pyongyang: A Central Military Commission meeting chaired by Kim Jong Un replaced Defence Minister No Kwang-chol with Kim Song-gi as part of a wider military reshuffle.
28 Aug – 3 Sep — No missile activity was recorded, following the roughly 10-missile short-range barrage of 20 August.
Ongoing — Russia: Assessments report North Korea expanding its support to Russia to include drone operators and a roughly 90-person ballistic-missile unit deploying to the Voronezh region.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Expect a return to launch activity once the US-ROK exercise season fully closes, with short-range and cruise tests and probable solid-ICBM engine or flight activity timed to political signalling, plus a possible parade or weapons reveal around the 9 September founding day or the 10 October party anniversary. Continued expansion of the Russia relationship — troops, missiles, now UAS operators — will keep hardware and doctrine flowing back to the peninsula, and Pyongyang will keep rebuffing President Lee's outreach. Kinetic DMZ escalation remains low-probability; the most dangerous scenario is a lethal grey-zone incident at the maritime boundary, with a seventh nuclear test a possible negotiating shock.

countries.name: Myanmar
incidents: 30 Aug — Vumkhum, Mindat Township, Chin State: Junta jets dropped four bombs on a village crowded with displaced people, killing eight civilians including a preschooler and wounding more than 15.
2 Sep — Irrawaddy River, Shwegu–Bhamo stretch: KIA and PDF forces attacked a junta river resupply flotilla, hitting up to four vessels and reportedly sinking one.
2 Sep — Mahlaing and Wetlet: Junta airstrikes struck resistance-held areas in the Mandalay and Sagaing regions.
Through Aug — Rakhine and Chin States: Monitors confirmed August civilian deaths from junta airstrikes exceeded 100, a pattern carrying into September.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained, deteriorating. Airpower-driven civilian killing will continue as the junta's primary tool, concentrated in Rakhine, Chin, Sagaing and the Mandalay-Kachin corridor, with monsoon river-resupply convoys to Bhamo a recurring flashpoint. The military-backed post-election government provides no course change. Expect a sustained 80–120-plus monthly civilian air-casualty tempo, further Arakan Army consolidation in Rakhine, possible junta ground pushes in dry-season prep from October, and a risk of strikes spilling toward the Bangladesh border and Chinese-interest infrastructure at Kyaukphyu; no credible ceasefire path exists in this window.

countries.name: Pakistan
incidents: 28 Aug — Kolpur, Balochistan: The BLA struck a Pakistani Army vehicle, part of a sustained late-August attack wave across the province.

1 Sep — Chagai and Pishin districts, Balochistan: Overnight security operations killed 21 militants — 11 at an extortion checkpoint on the N-40 highway and 10 TTP fighters at a customs compound — and six security personnel.
Ongoing — Khyber Pakhtunkhwa: TTP pressure continued alongside the BLA's geographically broad campaign, with AJK post-election grievances still a live unrest driver in Muzaffarabad.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. The BLA and BLF will maintain a high operational tempo — laborer killings, convoy IEDs, checkpoint seizures for extortion and complex 'Majeed Brigade' attacks — with continued spread from the Baloch core into Pishin, Killa Abdullah and Chaman and along the coastal CPEC axis. The army and Frontier Corps will keep responding with high-body-count clearance operations, drone strikes and cross-border strikes into Afghanistan that strain Islamabad-Kabul relations. TTP will maintain KP attacks and periodic mass-casualty strikes; CPEC-linked and Chinese-national targets remain high-risk. No prospect of political accommodation in Balochistan.

countries.name: India
incidents: 2 Sep — Imphal: Kuki-Zo legislators attended a Manipur Assembly session in person for the first time in more than three years, a modest de-escalation signal.

Late Aug – early Sep — Manipur: Kuki-Zo organisations announced a total shutdown of Kuki-Zo areas on 28 September and travel restrictions for 26–29 September, citing intelligence of possible attacks by Meitei armed groups.
Ongoing — Valley–hill fringe: Sporadic inter-community firing and arson continued, with the underlying dispute unresolved despite the elected state government.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained (watch); Manipur hill districts remain localised CRITICAL. The MLA return is positive optics but does not address buffer-zone security or displaced-population returns. Expect a spike in tension around the 28 September shutdown and continued low-level killings, drone and RPG use, and arson, with flashpoints around the Naga-civilian-killings investigation and any delimitation or electoral-roll moves. Elsewhere in India — Jammu and Kashmir, the Naxal belt — no window-specific escalation. The risk of a single high-casualty Manipur incident re-triggering wider valley unrest remains real, with added north-east exposure from Myanmar spillover.

countries.name: China
incidents: 29 Aug — Kinmen: Two China Coast Guard vessels intruded into Taiwan's restricted waters, among several incursions near Kinmen and Pratas during August.

August summary — Taiwan: The PLA flew 125 aircraft into Taiwan's ADIZ, continuing a marked 2026 decline from the post-2024 peak, while 150-plus non-warship vessels were logged around the island in the first three weeks.

Ongoing — Scarborough Shoal / Senkakus: The China Coast Guard sustained a record patrol tempo at Scarborough (near 2025's full-year total in the first half of 2026) and a near-daily presence at the Senkakus.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Beijing appears to be rebalancing coercion from PLA air sorties toward persistent maritime and coast-guard presence, exploiting the Western Pacific US carrier gap. Expect continued record China Coast Guard operations at Scarborough and around Pag-asa, more Kinmen grey-zone incursions, at least one snap PLA exercise around Taiwan — likely tied to the November referendum and local elections or a US arms announcement — and steady Senkaku pressure on Japan reinforced by China-Russia messaging. PLA sortie and vessel counts near Taiwan will likely stay elevated but below crisis thresholds; a collision or injury incident at Scarborough or Second Thomas Shoal is the main escalation risk.

countries.name: Taiwan
incidents: 27 Aug — Taipei: The Legislative Yuan passed an NT$240 billion special defence budget for unmanned systems procurement and domestic drone-industry development, alongside live-fire artillery drills integrating UAVs.
28 Aug — Taipei: The Central Election Commission approved a referendum, to be held alongside November local elections, on repealing the 'nuclear-free homeland' policy.
29 Aug — Taiwan: The navy completed upgrades to two Hai Lung-class submarines enabling Mk-48 Mod 6 torpedoes and sub-launched Harpoon.
24 Aug — Taipei: Prosecutors indicted an Nvidia manager and eight others for smuggling AI-chip servers to China via Japan and Indonesia.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Asymmetric build-out — drones, submarines, munitions — is accelerating with cross-party budget support, while PLA air presence stays at the reduced 'new normal' baseline with sustained naval presence and episodic surges tied to political triggers. The AI-chip smuggling probe will widen with more indictments and tighter export-control enforcement. Watch the November referendum and local elections as a likely trigger for a PLA response, continued US arms-transfer friction, the east-coast Pacific approaches where China is normalising operations, and undersea-cable interference near Matsu and Penghu.

countries.name: Philippines
incidents: Late Aug — Pag-asa (Thitu) Island and Scarborough Shoal: Sustained heavy China Coast Guard and PLA Navy presence was documented, with embedded reporting describing Chinese vessels visible in almost every direction off Pag-asa and a coast-guard helicopter conducting reconnaissance near the island.

Ongoing — West Philippine Sea: Coast-guard water-cannon, ramming and blocking tactics against BFAR and PCG resupply missions continued, with no discrete new clash confirmed in-window but pressure elevated by the US carrier gap.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained, aggravated by the US carrier gap. With no US carrier in theater, expect China to keep testing Philippine resolve at Pag-asa and Scarborough — blocking and shadowing, water cannon, possible landings on nearby unoccupied features, enforcement of the declared Scarborough 'nature reserve,' and pressure on Pag-asa resupply. Manila will respond with more frequent multilateral patrols with the US, Australia and Japan, transparency-initiative publicity, and hardening of Kalayaan features. There is a high risk of a ramming, water-cannon injury or blockade standoff that triggers Mutual Defense Treaty consultation debate, and domestic pressure for a firmer line will grow.

countries.name: South Korea
incidents: 31 Aug — Seoul: President Lee Jae-myung replaced six ministers, including the defence minister, amid his approval rating falling to a record low around 40%.
28 Aug – 3 Sep — A quieter inter-Korean week saw no new North Korean launches; Pyongyang confirmed its rejection of Lee's armistice-to-peace-regime proposal.
Ongoing — Seoul: Kimsuky and other North Korean cyber-espionage activity continued against ministries and defence firms amid Diplomatic Academy breach fallout.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Lee's domestic weakness constrains his engagement agenda; expect continued North Korean rebuffs and no inter-Korean channel. The Diplomatic Academy breach fallout will drive a government-wide credential reset, audits of contractor-run IT systems and likely additional disclosures of DPRK-linked intrusions. On the military track, expect episodic DPRK launches around any exercise or Trump-Kim signalling and GPS jamming affecting civil aviation and shipping near the NLL, plus friction over the pace and terms of OPCON transfer and any further US force-posture adjustments.

countries.name: Vietnam
incidents: 28 Aug – 3 Sep — South China Sea: The window was quiet, with Chinese patrols concentrated around Vietnamese-held Spratly features including Sand Cay, Namyit Island and Petley Reef; no in-window incident.
16 Aug — South China Sea: China's unilateral fishing moratorium expired and Vietnamese vessels resumed operations in contested waters.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. Hanoi continues its 'bamboo diplomacy' — deepening ties with Australia, the US, Japan, the Philippines and the EU while managing Beijing carefully and avoiding public confrontation. Expect continued Spratly outpost dredging and construction across all 21 held features, periodic low-key coast-guard standoffs near Vanguard Bank and around resumed fishing, and no alignment with Philippine-style publicity. Rising Chinese patrol density raises the odds of a maritime incident over the quarter, historically underreported by Hanoi; the probability of a serious clash stays low.

countries.name: Japan
incidents: 28 Aug – 3 Sep — Senkaku Islands: A record China Coast Guard presence continued as Tokyo advanced plans to counter China's armed coast-guard fleet.

Ongoing — Regional: The 2026 Defense White Paper framing of China as the 'greatest strategic challenge' and China, Russia and North Korea as a coordinating bloc continued to shape budget and posture decisions.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained; watch for a possible upgrade given rising rhetorical intensity. Tokyo accelerates its defence build-up — counter-strike missiles, south-western-island hardening, a higher budget share — and deepens minilateral ties including the Mogami frigate deal with Australia. Expect continued near-daily Senkaku incursions, periodic China-Russia joint air and naval activity near Japanese airspace, and a domestic nuclear-latency debate that Beijing and Moscow will exploit rhetorically. Friction with China over the White Paper language stays diplomatic; a coast-guard incident at the Senkakus, or a North Korean missile overflight, is the main escalation risk.

countries.name: Indonesia
incidents: 28 Aug – 3 Sep — Papua highlands: TNI operations against the TPNPB continued following the mid-August Puncak Jaya headquarters drone strikes, with no major new clash independently confirmed in-window.
17 Aug — Central Papua: Firefights around Independence Day left one soldier dead and two wounded, and a TNI task force killed three TPNPB members.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Expect sustained TNI drone and air operations and ground sweeps in Central Papua and the highlands, TPNPB ambushes and infrastructure attacks on the Trans-Papua road and telecom towers, and continued civilian displacement and rights complaints. The post-Independence-Day tempo typically eases but does not stop. The Prabowo government prioritises security consolidation and resource projects, which sustain grievances, and there is a risk of a mass-casualty incident — an aircraft downing, hostage-taking, or a strike causing civilian deaths — that internationalises the issue. Media and monitor access stays highly restricted.

countries.name: Thailand
incidents: 28 Aug – 3 Sep — Thai–Cambodia border: The Malaysia-brokered December 2025 ceasefire held with no new clashes; Cambodia continued pressing for a Joint Boundary Commission session while Thailand conditioned talks on demarcation mechanisms.
Through Aug — Chanthaburi province: Thai army border-fence construction opposite Battambang drew an ASEAN Observer Team inspection and Cambodian objections.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. The ceasefire is likely to hold through the period, sustained by ASEAN monitoring and mutual exhaustion after the July-December 2025 fighting. Main risks are a landmine casualty, a patrol clash near Ta Moan, Ta Krabey or Preah Vihear, or nationalist escalation in either capital. Border demarcation stays deadlocked; expect periodic troop-movement accusations and localised closures rather than renewed large-scale combat.

countries.name: Bangladesh
incidents: 1 Sep — Dhaka: Army chief Gen. Waker-uz-Zaman met Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus to discuss the military's role assisting civil administration ahead of national elections.
23 Aug — Dhaka: PM-designate Tarique Rahman's planned first visit to India was put on hold amid the Hasina-extradition standoff, with bilateral ties described as strained.
Ongoing — Dhaka: July Charter implementation remained deadlocked, with the BNP filing most of the dissent notes over the implementation mechanism.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. The BNP government under Tarique Rahman manages a fractious post-transition landscape: Charter-implementation disputes with former allies, Awami League proscription grievances, and economic strain. India relations stay cold over Hasina's continued political activity from Indian soil, and the stalled visit signals a prolonged freeze affecting trade, border, water and transit issues. The pre-election period will see rising political-violence risk, heavier military involvement in law and order, and campus and communal unrest; no single flashpoint is likely to breach MODERATE, but cumulative instability is rising.

countries.name: Sri Lanka
incidents: 28 Aug – 3 Sep — Nationwide: No security incidents occurred; the early-August prison riots did not recur and the domestic environment stayed calm.
31 Aug — PM Amarasuriya travelled to Bhutan for a regional summit.
8 Aug — Colombo: A prisoners' rights committee petition to the UN resident coordinator over deaths and abuses at four facilities remained outstanding.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained, trending toward a downgrade. Prison unrest is contained with no spillover, and no political or communal flashpoint is active; the baseline is stable under the NPP government. Residual risk comes from roughly 39,000 inmates against a 10,000 capacity and any IMF-linked austerity measures triggering protests. If calm continues through mid-September, a downgrade to LOW is defensible; the risk to watch is a large-scale riot or custodial-death incident that draws sustained international human-rights attention.

regions.name: Americas
overview: The US 'narco-terrorism' campaign is pivoting from kinetic pressure to resource and political consolidation: the 28 August US-Venezuela energy accord gave Washington majority control over fields holding roughly 65 billion barrels of reserves, landing the same week the Operation Southern Spear boat-strike toll held flat at about 227 killed in 68 strikes — the strikes paused while terms are locked in.

Hard-right militarised security governance is now the mainland norm — de la Espriella in Colombia, Noboa in Ecuador, Fujimori in Peru, Paz in Bolivia — all pursuing crackdown-first agendas with US alignment; Colombia's scrapping of 'Total Peace' and record airstrike body counts, including confirmed child casualties, mark the sharpest and most destabilising shift this week.

Caribbean state fragility is worsening independent of US action: Haiti's gang siege (Kenscoff massacre fallout, 2,600-plus newly displaced, an unresolved hostage crisis and December elections in doubt) and Cuba's collapsing grid under a total oil embargo remain on separate but critical trajectories, both with high near-term escalation probability.

A pro-Israel, anti-Iran realignment is entering regional foreign policy: Colombia lifted reciprocal visa requirements with Israel (1 September) and Peru severed ties with Iran (2 September), both citing Middle East escalation and Strait of Hormuz trade disruption, introducing energy-price and supply-chain exposure for the region.

countries.name: Venezuela
incidents: 28 Aug — Washington / Caracas: The US and acting President Delcy Rodríguez announced an energy accord giving Washington majority control over fields holding roughly 65 billion barrels of reserves, on a stated 25-year term.
29 Aug — Caracas: Simultaneous street protests against the oil deal came from both the democratic opposition and hardline Chavistas, the latter also demanding the release of Maduro and Cilia Flores.
30 Aug — Venezuela: Maduro resurfaced in social-media photos, the first sign of life since his January capture, as backlash to the deal grew.
2 Sep — Caribbean / Eastern Pacific: One year of Operation Southern Spear boat strikes was marked, with the cumulative toll holding at about 227 killed in 68 strikes and no new strikes in the window.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Overt US-Venezuela military confrontation has de-escalated into a US-backed negotiated transition, but the resource-transfer terms have united opposition and Chavismo against Rodríguez. Expect the boat-strike pause to hold while Washington finalises oil terms, with SOUTHCOM assets remaining offshore as leverage. The central risk shifts from external strikes to internal instability: contested legitimacy of the Rodríguez government, potential Chavista or military-hardliner fracture over the 'sell-off,' and episodic unrest in Caracas. Monitor for a formal transition roadmap or election announcement, Maduro's legal status in US custody, and any resumption of strikes if talks stall.

countries.name: Colombia
incidents: 29 Aug — Bogotá: President de la Espriella formally ended the Petro-era 'Total Peace' negotiating framework, removing the last negotiated off-ramp with armed groups.
31 Aug — Guaviare: A military airstrike on a FARC-dissident (EMC) camp killed about 20, with five captured and two minors rescued — the deadliest such strike in years.
31 Aug — Guaviare: Forensic authorities confirmed minors among the dead of the 27 August 'Operation Amón' strike near El Retorno, driving a national controversy over child casualties.
1 Sep — Los Patios, Norte de Santander: A car bomb at a police station near the Venezuelan border killed one civilian and wounded more than 11, preliminarily attributed to the ELN.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. The government's 'no truce' doctrine — a stated 15 operations in its first 100 days — will keep the airstrike tempo and body counts high, generating further child-casualty scandals, judicial challenges and international criticism while doing little to reduce ELN and FARC-dissident capability. Expect intensified guerrilla retaliation — car bombs, drone attacks, infrastructure sabotage — concentrated in Catatumbo, Norte de Santander, Cauca and the Guaviare-Amazon arc, plus spillover friction along the Venezuelan border. The economic-emergency decree faces Constitutional Court review, and quake reconstruction competes with security spending; with Total Peace dead, no de-escalation channel exists for the horizon.

countries.name: Haiti
incidents: 29 Aug — Kenscoff: Gangs released 13 of the 50-plus hostages seized in the 23–24 August massacre — six children and seven women — while a gang leader maintained his threat to execute remaining captives if police press the offensive.
29 Aug — New York: The UN Security Council was briefed on the Kenscoff massacre, with members pressing for rapid resourcing of the new Gang Suppression Force.
1 Sep — Kenscoff / Artibonite: Displacement from the Kenscoff attack passed 2,600 as armed groups also killed residents in homes and fields in the Artibonite farming belt.
Ongoing — Nationwide: Gang attacks intensified ahead of the 13 December elections as the US flight ban on Port-au-Prince remained in force.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained, worsening. The Gang Suppression Force handover from the Kenya-led mission is happening amid the worst attack surge of the year and with gangs holding hostages as leverage, making a decisive security improvement before December unlikely. Expect continued Viv Ansanm pressure on the Kenscoff and Pétion-Ville approaches, further Artibonite and Centre expansion severing more of the road network, mass-kidnapping tactics, and displacement climbing well past 1.5 million. A credible nationwide 13 December vote is now improbable across much of the country — expect a narrowed or postponed vote or a legitimacy crisis over the Transitional Presidential Council's mandate — while low-volume US TPS-end deportation flights continue.

countries.name: Cuba
incidents: 28 Aug – 3 Sep — Nationwide: No eighth national grid collapse was recorded, with the island still recovering from the 2–3 August total collapse amid prolonged localised blackouts and extreme heat.
Late Aug — Havana: Sporadic protest and police operations continued in neighbourhoods such as El Fanguito over blackouts and water outages.
20 Aug — Washington: Fresh US sanctions on 10 Cuban state firms and ICAP leadership continued to accelerate foreign-firm withdrawal.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Structural drivers are unchanged — near-zero oil imports with only one Russian tanker allowed through since January, generation running below half of demand, no financing. Another total grid collapse within the horizon is highly likely, each one now carrying rising risk of spontaneous cacerolazo protest and localised unrest that pushes the political-prisoner count higher. The 20 August sanctions will worsen fuel and food shortages. The regime's tools remain repression plus emigration as a pressure valve; the low-probability, high-impact scenario is a broad multi-province uprising on the scale of July 2021, most likely triggered by a prolonged nationwide outage during peak heat.

countries.name: Ecuador
incidents: 28 Aug – 3 Sep — Nationwide: The window was quiet on headline incidents; the state of emergency continued across about 10 provinces with homicide rates at record levels.
16–23 Aug — Beijing: President Noboa's eight-day state visit sought the lifting of shrimp-processor suspensions and mining and energy investment.
4 Sep — Guayaquil: Panama's president was due to meet President Noboa on trade and security cooperation.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. The militarised security posture and deepening US cooperation — warships and aviation at Manta, special-operations presence in Esmeraldas — persist without measurable reduction in gang violence. Expect continued high homicide tempo in Guayas, Los Ríos and El Oro, prison crises, periodic car bombings, and further publicised joint interdictions and possible US strikes on vessels off Ecuador's Pacific coast. Noboa will try to bank Chinese trade and investment concessions without provoking Washington, a balancing act opposition figures will keep attacking, and rights complaints over joint US-Ecuador operations will keep accumulating.

countries.name: Peru
incidents: 1 Sep — Lima: August inflation hit 4.44% year-on-year, the fastest since 2023, driven by electricity, gas and housing costs.
1 Sep — Nationwide: A 60-day state of emergency was declared across 893 districts in 22 regions plus Callao over El Niño risk.
2 Sep — Lima: Peru severed diplomatic relations with Iran, citing incitement of violence, IAEA obstruction and Strait of Hormuz disruption, while retaining consular ties.
25 Aug — Lima / Callao: A 24-hour transport stoppage by 11 unions cut more than 80% of service in protest at extortion and driver killings.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Fujimori's government combines a hard-line crime agenda — delegated decree powers, recurring states of emergency — with mounting economic strain from accelerating inflation and El Niño damage across 893 districts. Congress is likely to grant delegated powers in narrowed form, enabling a rapid succession of emergency decrees the Senate can later contest. Transport-sector extortion and driver killings will keep producing rolling strikes and localised states of emergency in Lima, Callao and Trujillo, with a militarised policing response of limited effect. The Iran break is low direct risk but adds energy-price exposure and aligns Peru with the regional pro-Israel bloc.

countries.name: Bolivia
incidents: 28 Aug – 3 Sep — Nationwide: No security incidents were reported in the window; analysts assessed President Paz had emerged stronger from the June blockade crisis.
Ongoing — Chapare: The 29 July arrest warrant for Evo Morales remained unenforced, with the June state of emergency running to 20 September.

Ongoing — Nationwide: Diesel-subsidy cuts under Decree 5676 and the IMF programme kept cost-of-living pressure high, with transport and rural federations threatening coordinated national blockades in October.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained, though the government's position has consolidated. The subsidy-cut agenda tied to the IMF programme guarantees recurring fuel shortages and blockade cycles into October, and Morales retains mobilisation capacity in the Chapare, but a repeat of the paralysing multi-week national blockade is less likely given the government's June success and the state-of-emergency precedent. Congressional approval of the IMF arrangement and the Investment Law is probable but slow. The highest-risk window is October, when transport and rural federations have threatened coordinated national blockades; a de-escalation to MODERATE is defensible only once that window passes without major unrest.

countries.name: Dominican Republic
incidents: 28 Aug – 3 Sep — Nationwide: No discrete security incident surfaced; mass expulsions of Haitians continued at roughly 1,000 a day alongside border-wall expansion.
20–21 Aug — Cap-Haïtien: The first US TPS-end deportees arrived in Haiti as Dominican expulsions ran in parallel, with rights groups documenting abusive detention conditions.
countries.coa: LOW maintained. The deportation campaign will almost certainly continue at its current pace through the fall, now compounded by the US ending TPS protections and beginning its own direct deportation flights to Haiti — a convergence of removal pressure onto a Haitian state already unable to secure Port-au-Prince. This raises secondary humanitarian and stability risk without materially changing the Dominican Republic's own low direct-conflict profile; watch for any spillover if Haitian gang control reaches the border departments of Centre and Nord-Est, and continued rights-group documentation of detention conditions as the main reputational risk.

countries.name: Jamaica
incidents: August — St Catherine North: Police recorded the first murder-free calendar month in 29 months.
3 Sep — Nationwide: RADA issued island-wide bushfire and drought warnings as routine violent crime and INDECOM investigations continued.
~10 Aug — Spur Tree Hill, Manchester: An off-duty road-rage shootout between two police corporals remained under INDECOM investigation.

Jamaica's pattern of steady, largely operationally-justified police confrontations continues, fitting the established profile of targeted suspect encounters rather than a broadening security crisis. The internal police-on-police shootout under INDECOM investigation could draw scrutiny if it reveals systemic firearms-discipline issues, but absent escalation this remains the lowest-priority file in the region; peak Atlantic hurricane season in September and October is the more material near-term risk to Jamaican stability.
